title: Radioactive Decay and Geologic Time
learningObjectives: Define half-life as the time required for exactly one-half of parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms at a constant rate
Use the equation N=N0*(1/2)^(t/T) to calculate the amount of a radioactive substance remaining after a given time
Explain how measuring parent and daughter isotopes helps assign numeric ages to boundaries on the geologic time scale using many samples

explanations.text: Radioactive decay from parent to daughter happens at a constant rate defined by half-life, which is the time needed for one-half of the parent atoms to decay.

evidence.quote: The change from parent to daughter happens at a constant rate, called the half-life.
The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the length of time required for exactly one-half of the parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms.

explanations.text: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, and each radioactive isotope has its own unique half-life as it converts to a daughter isotope.

evidence.quote: Isotopes of an element are atoms that differ from one another only in the number of neutrons in the nucleus.
Each radioactive isotope has its own unique half-life.

explanations.text: Measuring remaining parent atoms and new daughter atoms can be used to compute the age of a rock, but assigning a numeric age to a boundary on the geologic time scale requires many samples from different places.

evidence.quote: Many samples, usually from several different places, must be studied before assigning a numeric age to a boundary on the geologic time scale.
